title: Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge for Window cleaning (all heights)
audience: Owners of small Australian window cleaning businesses who need a base rate and a minimum charge before quoting
learningOutcomes: Separate billable hours from non-billable hours, and calculate the time available to bill.
Calculate a base hourly rate from your own costs and income target, then compare it with local evidence.
Set a minimum charge for short window jobs, such as a single pane or a track, and explain it before the visit.

instruction.heading: Factors that move the rate
instruction.body: A window rate depends on storeys and access, the skill of working safely at height, how far you travel, and the range of work you offer. A round that a client can book as exterior, interior and tracks in one visit saves the client time, which can support a higher rate. A narrow service in a crowded market may need a rate closer to local norms. Use the local evidence in the window CP-01 and CP-04 lessons and the window BP-05 lesson, not a national average. The lead-generation Melbourne hourly band for standard residential work is $42 to $84, averaging $58, and $84 to $210, typically $135, for high-rise or rope access (What's The Damage, verified November 2026). It is an estimate and not a published cost.

instruction.heading: Counting the hours that can be billed
instruction.body: Owners often price as though every paid hour can be billed. Travel, quoting, admin, marketing, training, equipment upkeep, sick days and leave are not billable. Estimate paid hours for a year, then subtract non-billable time to reach billable hours. Jobber puts billable time at about 60 to 80 per cent of working hours (published 5 November 2024, modified 20 July 2026). That is a general range, not an Australian figure, so check your own log against it. If only 60 of every 100 paid hours are billable, the costs of all 100 hours must come from the 60, so the rate is about 1.67 times the rate for a fully billable week.

instruction.heading: Building the rate from costs and income
instruction.body: Add the annual running costs of the window round, including insurance, registration, ladder and pole kit and its upkeep, the vehicle, phone, software, marketing and accounting, to the income you need. business.gov.au says on-costs such as superannuation, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure, so decide how each will be allowed for, and have a registered tax agent confirm the treatment for your situation. Divide the total by billable hours to get the base rate. Work backwards from a target income if that suits you: AIPT's guide divides a target income by working weeks and weekly hours, then adds tax and business costs. Review the base rate each quarter and compare it with what clients accept.

instruction.heading: Setting a minimum charge for short jobs
instruction.body: A single pane, a track or a small balcony still needs travel, set-up and admin. These do not shrink with the size of the job. Set a minimum that covers a short visit, and state it before the visit. Contractor+ suggests setting the minimum from the full cost of the visit, divided by one minus the target margin, so that travel, set-up and cleanup are covered. Its example figures are labelled illustrative and are not used here. Housecall Pro (country not stated) suggests a call-out or minimum covering travel, setup and admin; its figures are not used because the country is not stated.

procedure: Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract travel, admin, marketing, training and leave to find the billable hours.
List the annual running costs for the window round, including insurance, registration, equipment, vehicle, phone, software and marketing.
Add the income you need, with allowances for leave and tax confirmed by a registered tax agent.
Divide the total by billable hours to find the base rate.
Set a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up and admin for a short job, and state it in writing.
Review the rate each quarter, and record any change and the reason for it.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative only. A window cleaner's log shows that about 60 of every 100 paid hours can be billed, but the owner plans to set the rate as if every paid hour could be billed.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the effect on the rate if the wrong assumption is kept?
workedExamples.reasoning: Pricing as if every paid hour were billable understates the rate, because the costs and the income still have to come out of the hours that can be billed. On the owner's own log, the rate is about 1.67 times the rate for a fully billable week. The rate must be built from billable hours, then checked against the lead-generation Melbourne band and the minimum charge before it is published.

equipmentAndPpe: Log of paid and billable hours for one month
Price sheet with the base rate, the minimum charge and the review date

commonErrors.error: Setting a rate from a lead-generation band or a marketplace figure without checking your own costs.
commonErrors.prevention: Build the base rate from your own costs and billable hours, then compare it with local evidence.

commonErrors.error: Pricing as though every paid hour could be billed.
commonErrors.prevention: Subtract the non-billable time before dividing.

commonErrors.error: Taking short window jobs at the same price as a full round, without covering travel and set-up.
commonErrors.prevention: Set and state a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up and admin.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Price display rules come from the Australian Consumer Law. The ACCC says misleading price statements are prohibited, and a single advertised price should show the total including any fee. The ACCC guidance does not cover minimum or call-out charges, or what counts as a fair term. Check those points against current ACCC guidance or a legal adviser before publishing a price sheet.
Confirm the tax treatment of leave, superannuation and business costs with a registered tax agent.

Working at height affects the time and the minimum charge. Victoria's working-at-height rules were not checked in this draft, so check the Victorian rule with WorkSafe Victoria before you price any storey.

qualityStandard: Billable hours are calculated from a logged or estimated month, not assumed.
The base rate is built from the owner's costs and income target, and is compared with local evidence.
A minimum charge is set and stated before any short job.
documentationEvidence: Annual costs and income worksheet, with the source and date of each cost
Billable hours calculation showing the non-billable deductions
Price sheet showing the base rate, the minimum charge and the review date
summary: Price from billable hours, not from paid hours.
Build the rate from costs and a stated income target, then check it against local evidence.
Set and state a minimum charge for short window jobs.

knowledgeChecks.question: A window owner can bill only some of the paid hours. How should the rate be built?
options: From all paid hours, so the rate looks lower and so the client pays less per job
From billable hours, so the costs and income are covered by the work that can be billed
From the average published on a website and from the rate listed by the nearest competitor
From the rate the owner wishes the market would pay and the owner's own mood on the day

knowledgeChecks.question: Why set a minimum charge for a short window job, such as a single pane or a track?
options: Because short jobs need travel but no setup time at all and the admin takes no time
Because travel, setup and admin time does not shrink with the size of the job
Because clients expect every job to cost the same amount, whatever its size
Because a minimum charge replaces a written quote for every job the owner takes

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the best source for checking a window base hourly rate?
options: A single published national average from the largest trade body
The owner's own costs and billable hours, compared with local evidence
A friend's rate, without checking the costs or the local market
The rate shown on the first page of a bidding site this week

Housecall Pro, 'Flat rate vs hourly', https://www.housecallpro.com/learn/flat-rate-vs-hourly/, published 2 February 2025, updated 7 October 2025. Vendor page; country not stated; figures not used.

What's The Damage, 'Window cleaning cost Melbourne', https://whatsthedamage.com.au/window-cleaning-cost-melbourne/, verified November 2026. Lead-generation estimates of hourly bands; used as a sense-check only.
ACCC, 'Setting prices: what's allowed', https://www.accc.gov.au/business/pricing/setting-prices-whats-allowed, last modified 15 July 2026. Supports: misleading price statements are prohibited.

Business Victoria, 'Develop a pricing strategy', https://business.vic.gov.au/business-information/finance/pricing-for-profit/develop-a-pricing-strategy, no date shown. Supports: review prices about every three months.

Work Health and Safety (Managing the Risk of Falls at Workplaces) Code of Practice 2015, https://legislation.gov.au/F2016L00425/asmade/2016-03-30/text/original/epub/OEBPS/document_1/document_1.html, registered 2016. Commonwealth code; not Victorian law. Cited for the height point; the Victorian rule was not checked.

WorkSafe Victoria, news release on falls risks in the solar sector, https://www.worksafe.vic.gov.au/news/2026-08/crackdown-falls-risks-solar-sector, 26 August 2026. Supports: allowing workers onto a roof without adequate protection is unlawful, even with no incident. Aimed at solar; the principle is stated for any roof.
Note: minimum and call-out charge rules, price display beyond the ACCC pricing page, and tax treatment of leave and superannuation are UNCONFIRMED. No window-specific minimum charge was found.
